lede: Quadrature and cubature replace an integral by a weighted sum over a few nodes. The atlas collects the smallest known cubature rules with positive weights and nodes inside the domain, for degrees 1 to 30 (depending on the domain, up to the degree for which a rule is available) on the interval, triangle, square, tetrahedron and cube. Typical uses are the finite element method, multiple integrals and any computation where a function evaluation is expensive.

oqTri9:
Open question (triangle, degree 9): is N = 19 minimal? The proven lower bound is 17 (Möller).

17 and 18 nodes: 600 random and cannonball starts each, with nodes inside, nodes outside allowed, and arbitrary weights, found no rule; the same search finds the 19-node rule within 200 starts. With 18 nodes the solver drives one node far outside and its weight to 0, so effectively 17 nodes remain.

The next step of the moment method does not decide it: with free moments of degree 10 the discrete Gram matrix of the orthonormal polynomials of degree 5 can be made positive semidefinite of rank 2 (moment_relaxation.py), so 17 nodes are not excluded at that level. A proof needs the moments of degree 11 and 12 (flat extension), as for the cube at degree 6.
oqCube6:
Open question (cube, degree 6): is N_PI = 22 minimal, and is N_PO = 21 minimal? The proven lower bound is only dim P3 = 20.

21 nodes inside the cube: thousands of random starts found no rule. All 12 distinct 21-node rules found with positive weights (up to symmetry) have nodes outside the cube; the closest one reaches max|x| = 1.272 (the PO rule shown here).

20 nodes, anywhere: such a rule exists exactly if the moment matrix M(3) has a flat extension M(4) (Curto-Fialkow). This is a system of 75 quadratic equations in the 36 moments of degree 7. Numerically it has no real or complex solution, but no algebraic certificate of degree 4 or lower exists, so a proof needs heavier computer algebra (degree 6 or more).

For the disk, Easwaran, Fialkow and Petrovic (2006) proved the analogous 10-node case; the next case there is open as well.

notes.interval: On the interval the Gauss–Legendre rule is optimal: counting value, lower bound and Gauss product coincide, so no rule needs fewer than ⌈(n+1)/2⌉ nodes.
notes.triangle: The rules are at most 2 nodes above the counting value and never larger than the Xiao–Gimbutas rules. At degrees 3, 7, 10, 15, 17 and 18 to 20 they are smaller. The comparison is only partly fair, because the literature rules are fully symmetric. At the odd degrees 3, 5 and 7 the rules reach Möller's lower bound (4, 7 and 12 nodes), so they are minimal.
notes.square: At the odd degrees 9 and 11 the rules reach the Möller bound (17 and 24 nodes). Compared with the smallest known fully symmetric rules (for example 57 nodes at degree 17), the centrally symmetric rules here need fewer nodes (54). From degree 21 the rules lie at most 1 node above the counting value at even degrees and below it at odd degrees.
notes.tetra: The counting value is a good forecast here: for all degrees the rules are 0 to 5 nodes above it. Degrees 19 and 20 (389 and 446 nodes) are the most recently improved; the search there is not exhausted. The fully symmetric rules in the literature are larger (degree 9: 59, degree 10: 81). At degree 3 the 6-node rule is minimal among rules with positive weights (proof in the documentation; 5 nodes need a negative weight). At degree 5 the search found no rule with 13 nodes (980 starts, nodes outside allowed), and 12 nodes are excluded exactly for any real weights (documentation, tetra5_bound.py), so the bound is 13 and the gap to the 14-node rule is 1. At degree 7 no rule with 30 interior nodes was found (224 starts; with nodes outside, 30 exist).
notes.cube: The cube shows the widest gap between the Gauss product and the smallest known rules: from degree 10 the product needs more than three times as many nodes. Compared with fully symmetric rules (degree 9: 58, degree 15: 199) the centrally symmetric rules here are smaller (48 and 186). At degrees 3, 5 and 7 the rules reach Möller's bound for centrally symmetric domains (6, 13 and 26 nodes), so they are minimal.

exSub: The rules integrate functions that are not polynomials. The plot shows the relative error against the exact value, over the degree. The orange line is the computing accuracy; below it the error is only rounding noise. Square root and logarithm are shifted so that they stay finite on the whole domain, the branch point lies just outside. The error spans 16 orders of magnitude and therefore needs a logarithmic scale.

certH: Proof: rules lie near exact solutions
certSub: A rule whose moments are correct to 10<sup>−15</sup> is not yet an exact rule. Two checks look for an exact solution of the moment equations near the stored numbers. The Newton–Kantorovich certificate is computed in floating point with an estimated Lipschitz constant: strong evidence, but no proof. The interval proof (Krawczyk test with interval arithmetic, every rounding error accounted for, program tools/verify_rigorous.py) is a mathematical proof that an exact rule exists within the stated distance and that it has the stated quality (positive weights, nodes inside or outside).

exNnoteC: Only the minimal PI rules of the atlas and the Gauss product, each undivided and as a composite rule: the domain is split into k parts per direction (k^dim congruent cells; tetrahedra by red refinement), the rule is mapped onto every cell and the results are added up. The x axis counts function evaluations, i.e. nodes × cells; curves running past the right edge are cut there. The rounding bound is the one of the undivided rule. At equal node count the undivided rule of higher degree is usually ahead; within degree 30 composite rules win mostly only for the Runge function, and not on the tetrahedron.
